articles.title: GM wants drivers to take their eyes off the road by 2028
articles.summary: GM plans to debut eyes-off driving in the Cadillac Escalade IQ by 2028, but safety testing reveals how long distracted drivers take to regain control.
articles.body: Would you feel comfortable watching a movie while your car cruises down the highway at 70 mph? General Motors is betting that someday you will. The automaker plans to introduce technology in 2028 that could let drivers take their hands off the steering wheel and their eyes off the road. That means you could potentially answer emails, watch a show or attend a virtual meeting while your vehicle handles the driving. The technology is expected to debut in the Cadillac Escalade IQ electric SUV. However, GM still has plenty to prove before drivers can safely look away from traffic. The company is testing how people react when a vehicle suddenly needs their attention. That research could help GM determine how much warning drivers need before safely taking control. Join our upcoming CyberGuy LIVE class: 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money In this free live online class, Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will share five practical ways to protect your trip and your wallet this holiday travel season. You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Join us Saturday, October 31, at 11 AM ET / 8 AM PT. Register free now at CyberGuyLive.com. IKEA TURNS TO DRIVERLESS SEMIS WITH NOBODY IN THE CAB How GM plans to make eyes-off driving possible GM already offers Super Cruise, a hands-free driving system available on more than 20 models across Cadillac, Chevrolet, GMC and Buick. It can manage steering, acceleration and braking on compatible roads under certain conditions. However, drivers must continue watching the road and remain ready to take control. The next version of Super Cruise would remove that constant attention requirement when the eyes-off feature is active. GM plans to introduce it on compatible highways before eventually expanding to other roads. The system will use lidar, radar and cameras to monitor its surroundings. Turquoise lights on the dashboard and exterior mirrors will signal when eyes-off driving is available and active. GM says the technology could arrive as early as 2028. However, the launch depends on further development, safety testing and other requirements. Availability will also depend on state laws. GM's ambitions are also growing. On Oct. 21, the company announced plans to bring autonomous highway driving to its full-size SUVs and light-duty pickup trucks, including gas-powered vehicles. Those vehicles represent some of GM's biggest sellers. However, the automaker has not announced when the technology will reach those additional models. Why GM is putting drivers inside a virtual world Before asking drivers to trust a vehicle with their safety, GM wants to understand what happens when people stop concentrating on driving. At its Global Technical Center in Warren, Michigan, hundreds of volunteers have climbed into real GM vehicles, including the Cadillac Lyriq. However, instead of driving onto an actual highway, they enter an immersive simulator that recreates different road conditions. Researchers can introduce sudden traffic changes, construction zones and hazardous situations. Meanwhile, sensors monitor drivers' eye movements, heart rates and stress responses. The tests help GM understand how people behave when the technology encounters something unexpected. GM also tests its automated driving technology on closed courses and public roads with trained safety drivers. According to the company, its simulation tools can reproduce the equivalent of 100 years of driving in a single day. That gives engineers opportunities to study dangerous situations without exposing everyday drivers to those risks. Why Candy Crush is part of GM's driving tests Here's something I didn't expect to see in automotive safety research. GM is asking some participants to play Candy Crush while researchers study their reactions. The game creates an engaging distraction. Players become focused on improving their scores, which gives researchers a way to measure what happens when they must suddenly shift their attention back to driving. According to reporting by The Associated Press, Maureen August, a senior manager at GM Research & Development, explained that the game helps researchers draw participants into an activity before interrupting them. That interruption is especially important. Consider how long it takes to understand what's happening around you after you've been concentrating on your phone. Now consider making that adjustment while sitting behind the wheel of a moving SUV. At 70 mph, a vehicle travels roughly 103 feet every second. Even a five-second delay means it covers more than 500 feet. That's a lot of highway to travel while someone figures out why the car needs help. WHAT HAPPENS IF THE WAYMO COMPUTER FAILS? What happens if the car suddenly needs you to drive? This may be the biggest question surrounding GM's plans. What happens when an automated vehicle encounters a situation it cannot safely handle? Perhaps there's debris blocking the highway. Maybe road markings disappear during construction. An unexpected maneuver by another driver could also create a dangerous situation. GM's engineers are studying how much warning drivers need before taking control. Researchers also examine whether people understand the system's alerts and feel comfortable trusting the technology. However, an eyes-off system must be designed around the possibility that someone cannot respond immediately. That's why the vehicle's ability to handle unexpected conditions and safely manage a failed takeover becomes especially important. GM has not yet publicly detailed every situation its planned system will handle or exactly how it will respond when a driver fails to take over. How GM compares with Tesla and Ford Several automakers already offer systems that reduce the work involved in highway driving. However, their capabilities vary considerably. Ford's BlueCruise allows hands-free driving on compatible roads, but drivers must continue paying attention. Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised) can handle many driving tasks, although it still requires active human supervision. Mercedes-Benz previously introduced its DRIVE PILOT system, which allowed conditional eyes-off driving in limited situations. However, the automaker has since pulled back from that technology in the U.S. as it develops its next generation of automated driving systems. GM's larger ambition is to make eyes-off driving available at highway speeds across a broader network of compatible roads. The company hopes to expand the capability to additional models after the Escalade IQ. Will GM charge drivers to take their eyes off the road? There's a financial incentive behind the push toward automated driving. Automakers increasingly offer advanced features through paid software subscriptions. GM already charges for continued Super Cruise access after the included service period expires. According to the company's August 2026 update, equipped vehicles include three years of service, followed by plans starting at $39.99 per month. GM has not announced pricing for its future eyes-off technology. Some industry analysts believe drivers will be more willing to pay for technology that frees up their time behind the wheel. Still, there's a practical question for buyers. If you're already paying a premium for a luxury SUV, how much more would you be willing to spend each month to use its most advanced driving features? WAYMO RECALLS ROBOTAXIS OVER CONSTRUCTION-ZONE RISK What GM's eyes-off driving technology means to you If you're considering a vehicle with advanced driving technology, pay attention to what the manufacturer actually promises. Today's hands-free systems generally require you to keep watching the road. GM's planned eyes-off feature would allow you to look away only when the system is properly engaged under compatible conditions. Before paying for that capability, you'll want to know where it works and how the vehicle handles emergencies. It's also worth asking what happens if the system requests your attention while you're distracted. Also, don't overlook the ongoing cost. Subscription fees could make a vehicle more expensive to own than its original purchase price suggests. And remember, GM's planned system remains under development. Until a manufacturer explicitly authorizes eyes-off operation under the appropriate conditions, keep watching the road and follow the system's instructions. Kurt's key takeaways I love the idea of a less stressful drive, especially on those long stretches of highway where you're staring at the same traffic for miles. But handing over control is one thing. Taking my eyes off the road while traveling at highway speed is another. GM's research is encouraging because the company is studying how people actually behave when they're distracted. Still, I want to know what happens when the car encounters something it wasn't expecting. And if automakers plan to charge us every month for this technology, they'd better be able to show that it's safe and dependable. I'd be curious to try it, but I'd want a lot more evidence before settling in to watch a movie. Would you trust your car enough to watch a movie while it drives at 70 mph, or would you always want to keep an eye on the road? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: Lina Attalah: Egypt court fines journalist Lina Attalah and orders Mada Masr's closure
articles.summary: Amnesty International said the verdict against Attalah and independent outlet Mada Masr represented "a crushing blow to press freedom".
articles.body:
The editor-in-chief of the independent Egyptian news outlet Mada Masr was detained for several hours after a court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website and ordered its closure, her lawyers say.

Mada Masr said Lina Attalah was released once it paid the fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100) also handed down to her by the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court. It was the maximum possible penalty for the charge, which she had rejected.

Amnesty International said the verdict represented "a crushing blow to press freedom".

It comes only weeks after six journalists working for the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ).

President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi has overseen what human rights groups say is an unprecedented crackdown on dissent since he led the military's overthrow of his predecessor, Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohammed Morsi, in 2013.

Tens of thousands of people have been detained, mainly Brotherhood officials and supporters but also leading secular and liberal activists, media workers and academics.

Egyptian journalists from fact-checking website facing terrorism charges

AI 'SpongeBob' parody of problems in Egypt draws scrutiny of authorities

TV presenter among 12 sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case

The CPJ said Mada Masr, which was founded in 2013, was a vital source of critical reporting in Egypt and that it had long faced pressure from authorities over its journalism.

The site had repeatedly sought an operating licence from the Supreme Media Regulatory Council (SMRC) since a new media law was passed in 2018, but that its applications were either rejected or left unanswered, the media watchdog added.

Amnesty International said Lina Attalah had also faced "years of harassment and intimidation", including six criminal investigations over Mada Masr's reporting.

Last week, prosecutors summoned her for questioning over allegations of publishing "false news" and operating a website without a licence.

Mada Masr's lawyer said the investigation included a recent report that the website had published about a wave of protests in prisons across the country, as well as a letter from the SMRC regarding its legal status.

Attalah was released on bail and later referred to trial before the New Cairo Misdemeanours Court on the charge of operating a website without a licence.

During Tuesday's hearing, Judge Mohammed Mubarak ordered the courtroom to be cleared of everyone except Attalah, her eight-person defence team, and Hossam Bahgat, head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), an independent human rights group.

Bahgat told AFP news agency that security personnel then filed in before the judge announced that the court was denying several procedural requests made by the defence and appointing its own lawyer for Attalah.

"In a move that astonished all those present, the judge recorded in the official court minutes that the court had appointed a lawyer from the Lawyers' Syndicate to represent the defence," he said. "Lina herself spoke up to object to this lawyer being appointed to represent her, which the judge refused to record in the court minutes.

"In an even more shocking turn, the judge proceeded to dictate motions on behalf of this lawyer - who had not uttered a single word - and entered them into the official record," he added.

The judge then announced the fine for Attalah and ordered Mada Masr's closure "amid shouts and protests from the defence", before she was detained, according to Bahgat.

On Tuesday evening, Mada Masr said it had paid the full fine to the court and that Attalah was released after several hours in custody.

"During the release procedures, Attalah learned of a one-year prison sentence issued against her in absentia in 2024, on charges of publishing false news and managing an unlicensed website," it added.

"Her lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November."

Amnesty International warned that the court's verdict marked "a dark day for independent journalism" in Egypt and demanded that it be overturned.

"This draconian ruling is the culmination of years of relentless harassment and unjust proceedings designed to shut down one of the country's last remaining independent media voices," said the group's senior director for regional impact, Yasmine Ahmed.

"Lina Attalah should never have been prosecuted for exercising her right to freedom of expression and doing her journalistic job."

CPJ Regional Director Sara Qudah said: "If Egypt can put in custody one of its most respected editors and shut down her newsroom, no independent journalist in the country is safe. Attalah must be released immediately, and Mada Masr must be allowed to keep reporting."

articles.title: Let them eat cheesecake! Obama’s dig at gilded Trump White House causes MAGA meltdown
articles.summary: TOI correspondent in Washington: American fast food chain Cheesecake Factory has spent decades perfecting the art of serving customers an expansive menu
articles.body: TOI correspondent in Washington: American fast food chain Cheesecake Factory has spent decades perfecting the art of serving customers an expansive menu in portions that suggest they may never eat again. It has achieved something even more remarkable now: become a central character in the long running Trump-Obama feud that has devolved into a culinary spat wrapped in a culture war.The MAGA boss on Monday went after Obama, calling him a “lousy president,” after his predecessor mocked Trump’s obsession with a White House makeover, likening its gilded accents and gold platings to a Cheesecake Factory that Saddam Hussain may have opened. Peeved at the perceived slight to upgrades he thinks are required to restore the White House to pristine glory, but which critics think are gaudy and garish, a clearly annoyed Trump, in a lengthy rebuttal, said Obama was “not a smart guy” because he did not recognise the importance of showcasing class and quality.Also Read: Obama unloads on Trump while stumping for Democrats ahead of midtermsIt was a remarkable amount of presidential indignation to expend over a joke invoking comparisons to restaurant chain famous for serving enough food to require a congressional inquiry into portion control. It was also cue for Trump’s MAGA minions to order the outrage platter, with extra umbrage on the side, by seizing on Cheesecake Factory’s iconic status as one of the top family restaurants in middle America, a place that makes a glutton’s pulse quicken and arteries thicken.Conservative commentator Scott Jennings jibed that a man like Obama, who “makes speeches for 500k a pop, hasn’t eaten dinner that costs less than $250 in a year, has never been in a Cheesecake Factory,” was being condescending towards Americans who are not part of the elite class. Radio host Clay Travis recalled that eating there had been a special occasion for his family, as it remains for millions of others.And just to drive home the point, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, a billionaire former hedge-fund manager, duly dined at a Washington-area Cheesecake Factory, emerging to tell a conveniently waiting cameraman the “Martha’s Vineyard set” (Obama and his ilk) should give the restaurant a try. Criticism of the place that occupied a storied place in Middle America’s heart had come from a man whose presidential library resembled “Darth Vader’s tomb,” Bessent jibed. The White House itself joined the food fight, posting a list of Trump’s accomplishments in a format that resembled Cheesecake Factory’s menu.Obama’s defenders, trying to forestall the “deplorables” debacle that convulsed America (after Hillary Clinton characterised Trump supporters in those terms in 2016) insist the point was not that Cheesecake Factory patrons are deplorable or declasse or that the food is beneath liberals. He was making fun of Trump’s fixation on turning the People’s House into a monument to his own tacky aesthetic preferences - and the time and energy the president seems to devote to discussing the makeover while voters worry about prices, housing and healthcare.While conceding that Trump has a legitimate point when he says the White House should be clean, well maintained and beautiful, they argued the question is one of proportion. If Obama had compared the White House to French Laundry, a rarefied Michelin-star California restaurant, the snobbery charge might have had more seasoning; Cheesecake Factory, they acknowledge, is practically a national dialect.But when a President devotes excessive attention to gold trim, ballroom plans and reflecting pool, as Trump is doing to the point of making it a fetish amid ongoing war and economic crisis, they say the optics become cheesy. The MAGA supremo may regard the work as a labour of love; but right now critics see a commander-in-chief who seems preoccupied with cushions and drapes and upholstery - while the house is on fire.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2021, an Indiana mother and her teenage son lost contact after he moved away with his father; she later showed a court about 25 unanswered texts, and an October 26 ruling said she need not pay his college expenses
articles.summary: An Indiana mother who has had no contact with her teenage son for four years does not have to pay for his university education, an appeals court has ruled.
articles.body: An Indiana mother who has had no contact with her teenage son for four years does not have to pay for his university education, an appeals court has ruled. The Court of Appeals of Indiana upheld a lower court decision that found the son had rejected his relationship with his mother. Under state law, this gave her a complete legal defence against being forced to pay for his education after high school. The ruling in case number 26A-DC-01758 (Jonathan M. Pratt v. Jamie L. Pratt) ends the father's legal attempt to make his former wife contribute to their son's higher education costs.Family breakdown and relocationAccording to court records from the Howard Circuit Court, Jonathan M. Pratt and Jamie L. Pratt ended their marriage in November 2020. They initially shared physical and legal custody of their son, who was born in January 2007. The family situation changed in July 2021, when Mr Pratt moved to Georgia with their son, who was then 14 years old. Mrs Pratt stayed in Indiana. After the move, the Howard Circuit Court changed the custody arrangement. Mr Pratt received sole legal and physical custody, while Mrs Pratt was allowed to spend time with her son by mutual agreement. However, after the move to Georgia in 2021, Mrs Pratt did not have any further parenting time with her son.Unanswered messages presented as court evidenceWhen the son turned 18 in January 2025, Mr Pratt asked the court to order Mrs Pratt to help pay for their son's education after high school as he prepared to graduate. During a hearing in July 2025 before Special Judge Douglas A. Tate, the court heard different accounts of why the mother and son had stopped communicating. Both Mrs Pratt and her son agreed that they had not spoken to or seen each other since 2021. The son testified that his mother had not contacted him during those four years. However, Mrs Pratt presented electronic evidence showing that she had tried to reach him. Photographs of text messages submitted as evidence showed that Mrs Pratt had sent around 25 messages to her son between 2021 and 2025. One of those messages was sent directly to him on his 18th birthday. Her son did not reply to any of the messages.Trial court rules on relationship repudiationIn May 2026, the Howard Circuit Court issued its decision. It ruled that Mrs Pratt did not have to pay for college because her son had rejected his relationship with her. Mr Pratt appealed, arguing that the lower court had wrongly considered his son's failure to respond while he was still a minor living under his father's care and influence. Writing for the unanimous appeals panel, Judge Scheele rejected the father's argument and upheld the lower court's decision. Judges Brown and Kenworthy agreed with the ruling.Legal standard for parental college contributionUnder Indiana law (Ind. Code § 31-16-6-2), parents are not automatically required to pay for their children's education after high school. State courts can order parents to provide financial support for further education, but a child's rejection of a relationship with a parent can serve as a complete legal defence against such an order. In the opinion, Judge Scheele referred to earlier court decisions, Lovold v. Ellis and Messner v. Messner. These cases define repudiation as a child's complete refusal to take part in a relationship with a parent. The appeals court also addressed behaviour that begins before a child turns 18. The judges noted that although repudiation mainly concerns an adult child's behaviour after turning 18, courts can consider actions that started during the teenage years if the behaviour continues without change into adulthood.The opinion referred to the trial judge's original findings. Special Judge Tate stated: "While the court will tend to believe that a fourteen year old child ignoring his mother may be done at the influence of his father, not responding to your mother's birthday wishes, or providing your mother with updated contact information when you turn eighteen, is an adult decision and a clear repudiation of that parent." The appeals panel concluded that the trial court had acted within its authority by accepting Mrs Pratt's documented text messages as more reliable evidence than her son's testimony."By college age, children of divorced parents must be expected to begin to come to terms with the reality of their family's situation," Judge Scheele noted, quoting an earlier appeals court decision, McKay v. McKay. articles.title: Communication complaints after storm hits Aurigny flights
articles.summary: The Guernsey-based Airline says safety is its priority and it did contact passengers.
articles.body:
Air passengers said they were frustrated about delays and cancellations to their travel plans caused by Storm Austen when high winds grounded aircraft.

Liv Bichard was planning to take an Aurigny flight from Guernsey to attend an important family event.

She said her Aurigny flight was cancelled and she rebooked "and it just kept cancelling and they didn't warn me". Others also complained about what they said was a lack of communication.

The airline's chief commercial officer Philip Saunders said it did contact passengers and said safety was the firm's top priority.

Bichard told BBC Guernsey she had planned to fly to Southampton on Friday and then booked to Gatwick, before rebooking a flight on Saturday evening.

She said it would have helped "if they sent out more updates by email or text message".

She headed to the airport only to discover her flight was cancelled.

Bronwen Dudley-Owen also said she was frustrated with the level of communication.

She was due to fly to Paris to attend a funeral with a return flight via London over the weekend.

She asked the airline what she should do as Guernsey Airport was due to be closed, but said she was told by Aurigny's call centre the flight would be running but the Aurigny office said it would not go.

She said: "I'm absolutely baffled as to why they didn't let their customer support team know what was going on on the ground."

She added: "I've had no communication whatsoever. The whole system needs to be reviewed."

Saunders said the company regretted the delays and cancellations at the start of the autumn half-term getaway on an "extremely challenging weekend".

He said the "first priory as an airline is to always put safety first" and travel conditions "were outside of the limits possible for our aircraft over the weekend".

Aurigny operated 50% of the services on Saturday and "pretty much all of the network" on Sunday, Saunders added.

He said Dudley-Owen's flight had not been cancelled when she contacted the call centre and agents "provided her with the correct latest information we had available".

"The reality is that the situation was fluid and that operational circumstances change and evolve in storms of this nature," he added.

He said Aurigny issued updates on its website about the airport closure and sent emails and texts to passengers.

The airline also "unusually" suggested customers accepted refunds over the challenging weather conditions.

Saunders added aircraft were moved off-island to avoid the worst of the weather and it would take several days to clear the backlog of delays.

Saunders said: "We are confident that we sent cancellation messages to all passengers."

He said travel agents were responsible for contacting passengers who booked through them "and there are legal limits as to the communication the airline can undertake directly with the passenger, for whom in many cases we would not have contact details for".

articles.title: US Justice Dept asks Washington state not to count ballots from possible noncitizens
articles.summary: Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department has asked Washington state not to count any mail ballots received from more than 400 residents who it says may n...
articles.body:
FILE PHOTO: New banners depicting U.S. President Donald Trump are hung on the Department of Justice building in Washington

Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US Justice Department has asked Washington state not to count any mail ballots received from more than 400 residents who it says may not be US citizens, opening a ‌new front in the Trump administration's push to expand control of election administration ahead of the November 3 midterms.

The ‌letter, which resembled a request earlier this month that California not count any ballots received from around 20,000 alleged noncitizens, marked an escalation in the ​Trump administration's pressure on state election officials over alleged noncitizen voting. Multiple state audits and independent studies have found that voter fraud, including voting by noncitizens, is very rare and has not affected election outcomes.

The pressure campaign is a rare intervention by the Justice Department in the voting process in the weeks before an election. President Donald Trump's fellow Republicans are locked in a tight ‌battle to retain slim majorities in both chambers ⁠of the US Congress, and centrist Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez's campaign to hold onto her southwest Washington seat is one of 10 key races that could decide control of the US House of ⁠Representatives.

In the letter dated October 26, the top federal prosecutors in Seattle and Spokane asked Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs, the state's top elections official, to determine whether the more than 400 people were in fact US citizens and to not count their ballots ​until ​their citizenship was determined. The letter said the Justice Department would ​seek "emergency relief" if the state could not take those ‌actions by noon local time (1900 GMT) on Wednesday.

There were 5 million registered voters in Washington state as of 2024, according to the secretary of state's office.

In a statement, Hobbs said his office would only respond to requests that follow due process.

"The timing of this request — one week before the General Election — is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results," Hobbs said.

A Justice Department spokesperson said, "With his (Hobbs') help, we can ensure that only American citizens vote in Washington's elections."

In California, after state ‌election officials said complying with the Justice Department's demand would be ​impractical and questioned the accuracy of its information on alleged noncitizens, federal prosecutors ​filed a lawsuit seeking to block the state from ​counting any ballots received from the alleged noncitizens.

A hearing is scheduled in that case for 1 ‌p.m. PDT (2000 GMT) on Tuesday before US District ​Judge David Carter in Los Angeles. ​A federal appeals court on Monday night denied the Justice Department's request to block California from counting any ballots before Carter had the chance to rule.

Democrats and voting rights advocates say federal data on citizenship is often outdated, ​meaning naturalized citizens registered to vote are ‌often mistakenly flagged as noncitizens.

In its letter to Washington state officials, the Justice Department acknowledged that some ​of the individuals flagged as possible noncitizens may have since naturalized, but it did not say how many.

(Reporting ​by Luc Cohen in New York; Editing by Bill Berkrot)

articles.title: Police failings in friends' death on Yr Wyddfa could risk lives, coroner warns
articles.summary: Jayden Long and Eddie Hill died after police failed to adequately escalate a dropped 999 call.
articles.body:
More people could die on remote mountains unless police do a better job in responding to dropped 999 calls, a coroner has warned.

The bodies of friends Eddie Hill, 20, and Jayden Long, 19, both from Dereham, Norfolk, were found on a mountain ridge in Eryri, also known as Snowdonia , on 19 February, a day after a call from Long to North Wales Police was disconnected.

Officers did try unsuccessfully to call him back, but then made "limited" efforts to find out who owned the phone and took more than three hours to alert mountain rescue, assistant coroner Sarah Riley said.

North Wales Police said it had taken steps to strengthen its policies and procedures.

Hill and Long died in extreme winter conditions on Crib y Ddysgl, a ridge that peaks at 1,065m (3,494ft), less than a mile north of Yr Wyddfa's summit and linking it to the notoriously narrow ridge of Crib Goch.

A Prevention of Future Deaths report said police received a discontinued call from Long's mobile phone at 16:27 GMT on 18 February.

A playback captured him saying "hello" and "can you hear me?" before the call was lost.

The mountain rescue team told an inquest into their deaths that it did not have enough information about the location or nature of Long's 999 call to act immediately.

After further inquiries, including making contact with family members, mountain rescue teams and a coastguard helicopter searched the last known position of the two men but found no trace.

A decision was made to continue the search at first light.

A search and rescue dog team joined the mountain rescue teams for the search on the following morning, when the walkers' bodies were found.

The coroner identified several areas of concern following the inquest, including a lack of guidance or training for staff dealing with calls from remote mountainous locations and inadequate systems for sharing lessons learned from the incident.

"Unless action is taken to address the above concerns then there is a significant risk of future deaths," Riley said.

North Wales Police said it amended its communications centre policy in September 2026 to include specific guidance on handling silent or disconnected 999 calls from remote or mountainous locations.

Call handlers are now expected to consider alerting mountain rescue teams where a caller's location can be confirmed and, learning from the incident has been shared with communications staff.

The force said it hoped the response would "provide reassurance that the concerns identified have been addressed and that lessons arising from this tragic incident have been recognised and acted upon".

articles.title: Worker at US embassy in London investigated over abuse images is senior Air Force member
articles.summary: The BBC has been told Lt Col Michael Morris, who was flown out of the UK before being questioned by police, is under investigation.
articles.body:
A US embassy staffer accused of possessing and distributing child sex abuse material, but left the UK before he was questioned by British police, is a high-ranking member of the US Air Force, the BBC has been told.

The BBC understands he is Lieutenant Colonel Michael Morris, who worked as an assistant military attaché at the embassy in south-west London.

He was questioned by American authorities after investigators alleged his US-based brother Benjamin Morris had shared child abuse material with him.

Benjamin Morris, 33, is facing trial in the US state of Illinois for the possession and dissemination of child sexual abuse material, which he denies.

The Rock Island County State Attorney, Dora Villareal, told the BBC the allegations against Benjamin Morris relate to a period between March and April 2026.

His brother, Lt Col Michael Morris, was flown out of the UK in August on a civilian flight without first being questioned by British police.

While not a diplomat, it is understood he enjoyed the umbrella of diplomatic protection.

In September, the US embassy confirmed to the BBC that authorities are investigating the allegations and they reassigned the staff member to the US while inquiries continued.

A spokesperson for the US Air Force has since told the BBC: "Charges have been preferred against Lt Col Michael Morris, currently assigned to the Air Force District of Washington.

"The charges and evidence will be reviewed to determine whether the case should be tried by court-martial."

The US Air Force said "charges are merely allegations and the Department of the Air Force member is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty".

The spokesperson said a military hearing was due to take place in November at Joint Base Andrews near Washington DC, and Lt Col Morris will only enter a plea if the matter is referred to court-martial - a formal military criminal trial.

The US Embassy in London previously said it "expects all personnel to adhere to the highest standards of conduct, and we take these allegations seriously", adding it "quickly informed UK law enforcement and took swift action".

The Metropolitan Police said: "We have been liaising regularly with the US authorities since they made us aware on Tuesday, 25 August of their investigation into suspected offences relating to indecent images of children.

"We are aware that charges have been brought in the US in relation to this case and that legal proceedings are ongoing. We remain in contact with the US authorities".

A spokesperson for the UK government said: "We expect all foreign diplomats in the UK to abide by our laws, in the same way we expect all UK diplomats to do so when posted overseas.

"As a US investigation is ongoing, it would not be appropriate to comment further at this stage."

The BBC understands the government remains in close contact with the US Embassy, including at a ministerial level.

articles.title: Ash Dykes completes Congo Basin expedition after going 'missing' for 24 hours
articles.summary: Ash Dykes is trying to complete six back-to-back expeditions in a variety of extreme environments.
articles.body:
An adventurer has completed the first leg of his latest challenge after losing contact with his UK team for almost 24 hours.

Ash Dykes, 35, from Old Colwyn, Conwy, holds five world records but his most recent quest was the first of six back-to-back expeditions he will take on in extreme environments.

Dykes encountered elephants, gorillas and was chased by "killer" bees as he rowed more than 434 miles (700 km) along rivers in the Congo Basin, central Africa.

Towards the end of the journey, Dykes' portable satellite kit lost power. He said: "My parents and fiancée were worrying but as soon as I had a bit of signal I made sure I got in touch".

In his latest Project 6 challenge, Dykes will attempt six expeditions in very different locations.

He has previously walked 4,000-miles (6,437km) along the length of China's Yangtze River in 2019 and kayaked the length of the Coppename river in Suriname from source to sea in 37 days

On "going missing", Dykes said his "power bank just shut down".

"We were underneath the jungle canopy, because we were staying with a small community, and then it took me about 20 hours before I could get out the first message," he said.

As the adventurer is sharing expeditions "live", he said he had learned lessons from the experience going forward.

He said: "I don't think the world's ready for a truly live expedition so I've learned from that...

"If I lose contact again with the team, we have to keep it within the team because I do know that that hit alarms and a lot of people were stressed and panicked. So it's important to make this as live as possible, but moving forward, it can't be that live anymore."

During the adventure, Dykes said his biggest fear was not the danger posed by wildlife or disease, but the extreme heat during many hours of kayaking in rivers home to crocodiles and hippos with no shade.

He said: "We took the warnings seriously. Experience means listening to local advice, reading the conditions and making the decisions that get your team through safely."

For the explorer, the main highlight was spending time with the Baka tribe, a semi-nomadic indigenous ethnic group.

They demonstrated their hunting prowess which involves trapping animals in netting set up around the jungle.

"They were amazing, they took us under their wings, they showed us how they survive, how they hunt, how they gather," Dykes said.

"They took us to an area where we saw a group of gorillas within Sanga National Park. I was about five metres away from silverback."

Dykes was joined on his trek by local guide Obed Temba Tuyumvire as well as videographer Will Perez, who has been helping chart the journey with regular social media posts.

His popularity on TikTok has soared following his latest adventure.

Dykes said: "It felt like the world was on the river with us."

But he added some followers were disappointed in the lack of drama.

"Everyone wanted that excitement, that danger, but if something was to happen, I'd be criticised: 'this is dangerous'.

"Now that I've made it unscathed, everyone's like: 'It's easy, there were no crocs'.

"So there's no true winning when you go that viral."

He said he lost 11lbs (5kg) during the trip, as he was relying mostly on ration packs of food.

In a social media post to mark the end of the first stage of Project 6, Dykes said: "It's been a lot. We've faced ups and downs - seen some crazy wildlife, but more importantly we've survived."

Dykes said he would reveal the second stage of Project 6 next week, and hinted it would be somewhere "a lot colder" than the Congo Basin.

articles.title: A Court of Splintered Harmony fans queue for new Sarah J. Maas book
articles.summary: Some fans take the week off to read the latest instalment of the A Court of Thorns and Roses series.
articles.body:
As I arrive at Waterstones in York shortly before 08:00, there is already a queue forming outside the bookshop.

Fans of Sarah J Maas's bestselling A Court of Thorns and Roses (ACOTAR) series are waiting eagerly to get their hands on the latest instalment.

Among them is Olivia Bray, 28, who has spent more than a decade immersed in the American author's fantasy world.

For Bray, the appeal goes beyond magic, romance and fantastical kingdoms. It is the feminism running through Maas's books that has kept her coming back.

And with the release of A Court of Splintered Harmony, Bray is prepared to put real life on hold, having booked an entire week off work to give herself time to recover from whatever awaits her between the covers.

"I'll be done [with reading] by tomorrow," she said. "I've just got the whole week off in case it's traumatising."

Set in the fictional world of Prythian, the series has amassed millions of fans across the world.

The series follows Feyre Archeron, a young huntress drawn into the dangerous world of the fae, where she navigates political intrigue, war and romance.

There have been five books so far, A Court of Thorns and Roses (2015), A Court of Mist and Fury (2016), A Court of Wings and Ruin (2017), A Court of Frost and Starlight (2018), and A Court of Silver Flames (2021).

A Court of Splintered Harmony, the sixth book in the best-selling series, was released on Tuesday - five years after fans last heard from the characters.

Another ACOTAR fan, 22-year-old Abigail Wright, hoped to finish the book on release day, which coincided with her day off, before returning to work.

She said the books were her "gateway back into reading" aged 19.

Like Bray, Wright believed the recurring theme of female empowerment was a key part of its appeal.

"I think it's so popular because, yes, the romantic side of it is very good, but the strong women you see in the books are just a way to make other young women feel really empowered," said Wright.

"It just gives them a sense of power and [makes them] see you can start from nothing, like Feyre does, and just make your way up… you don't need a man to do all these things for you, you have the power to do anything you want to do."

Gabriella Booth, 29, was introduced to the series in 2013, but attributes ACOTAR's explosion in popularity to both the pandemic and "BookTok" - a TikTok community dedicated to sharing what people are reading and writing.

"The characters in general are so easy to read about. You can relate in different parts to a lot of them, I find," said Booth.

"For me, I love the fantasy world - that's something I've loved reading growing up. So, to have that combined with the romance side of everything... there's something that's just so exciting to read about."

Booth has previously taken time off work to read new releases and plans to do so when the seventh ACOTAR book is published in January.

However, on this occasion, she hopes to finish A Court of Splintered Harmony after work.

Alice Boyce, a bookseller at Topping and Company Booksellers on Museum Street in York, said ACOTAR fans had made their way straight up to the science-fiction area of the store as soon as doors opened at 09:00.

"People are really enthusiastic; we've had emails saying, 'can you put a copy aside for me?', and last night we had people asking to put it on pre-order."

An ACOTAR fan herself, 26-year-old Boyce said she felt she could truly disconnect when she read the books.

"You can dive into books and just escape a little bit," she added.

Events were held across the UK, including in Wolverhampton and Northern Ireland , to mark the new book's release, with Waterstones on York's Coney Street hosting its first ever midnight release event.

Eighty ACOTAR fans, some of whom were dressed as their favourite characters, attended the event, while 100 members of the fandom flocked to a party in Wolverhampton.

Organiser Holly Fellows, from Redditch, told the BBC people were "ecstatic" when the book was finally released.

"The community was just lovely, it was so nice to see everybody come together and fan-girl over a book," Fellows said.

Fellows, who booked the day off work to read the book, said she was already through the first chapter.

"It sounds like it's going to be incredible", she said.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme on Tuesday, Abi Fraser, owner of the Throne and Heart bookshop in Market Harborough, Leicestershire, where a release party was also held, said: "We had about 45 people in the bookshop to celebrate the midnight release.

"We had quizzes, we had games, we had a countdown to midnight - there is a real community vibe to the fandom... it's fantastic."

Elizabeth Vaziri, commissioning editor at Voyager and Magpie at the publisher Harper Collins, told the programme fantasy had "always been a portal for escapism".

Combined with romance, Vaziri said the "romantasy" genre had "given people a safe place to navigate relationships or sexuality".

articles.title: Nigerian controversial Islamic cleric Yahaya Masussuka shot dead in Katsina state
articles.summary: Yahaya Masussuka had posted videos in which he rejected some elements of mainstream Islam.
articles.body:
A controversial Islamic cleric in Nigeria has been murdered outside his home in the northern state of Katsina.

Two assailants arrived on a motorcycle and shot Yahaya Masussuka in the town of Dutsin-Ma as he was saying goodbye to visitors on Monday evening, sources told the BBC.

The 47-year-old preacher and one of his guests, who was also shot, were rushed to hospital but both were pronounced dead by the attending doctor, police said.

It is not clear why Masussuka was targeted, but the cleric had received death threats on social media where he posted videos in which he rejected some elements of mainstream Islam, including what happens to people after their death.

It is widely believed in Islam that a person's soul will be questioned in the grave by two angels. If they answer correctly, their soul sleeps peacefully until the day of judgement - if not it will be tormented.

This understanding comes from what is known as the Hadith, a collection of texts believed to be the spoken words and actions of the Prophet Muhammad.

This serves as a key source of Islamic knowledge to help interpret the Quran, the central religious text of Islam.

But Masussuka based his teachings mainly on what was in Islam's holy book, questioned some of the hadiths - and did not believe that the dead were reawakened and questioned.

He was once jailed for nine months because he teased some respected scholars over their belief in this hadith and other teachings.

Masussuka, who had two wives and seven children, began preaching at the age of 13 in Quranic schools.

He later attended Al-Azhar University in Egypt and later went to Oman for further studies.

At his home, he had a studio where he would record videos of his teachings for broadcast on social media for his followers.

The cleric was also outspoken about violent extremism, radicalisation and openly advocated for interfaith dialogue and peaceful coexistence between Muslims and Christians, who make up nearly equal parts of Nigeria's population.

Thousands of Christians and Muslims have been killed in ethnic and religious violence here over the past 25 years.

For Masussuka's efforts, Nigeria's Network for Good Governance and Transparency honoured him with a Peace Ambassador Award last year.

Six other prominent Muslim preachers have been murdered over the last two decades in northern Nigeria - several targeted by Boko Haram for criticising the jihadist group that began its insurgency in 2009.

Founded in north-eastern Nigeria, it opposes Western culture, education, the secular government - and its political goal is the creation of an Islamic state.

articles.title: An Irish dairy farmer devoted only 1.5 acres of his 110-acre holding to 1,008 solar panels, kept sheep grazing underneath and secured a 15-year electricity agreement to supply power equivalent to about 150 homes
articles.summary: An Irish dairy farmer has turned a small part of his land into a commercial clean energy project, setting a national example of how farms can earn income
articles.body: An Irish dairy farmer has turned a small part of his land into a commercial clean energy project, setting a national example of how farms can earn income from renewable power. Sean Keating, a farmer in Meadstown, Kildorrery, County Cork, used just 1.5 acres of his 110-acre farm to build Meadhill Solar Farm. The project is the first operational solar farm in Ireland to receive support under the government's Small-Scale Renewable Energy Support Scheme (SRESS). The ground-mounted solar farm has 1,008 Longi 645W solar panels installed by PV Generation. The system can produce up to 650 kWp of electricity and is expected to generate between 600 and 650 megawatt-hours of clean power each year. This is enough electricity to supply around 150 local homes while preventing an estimated 100 to 120 tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions annually.Dual land use keeps livestock grazingInstead of removing farmland from agricultural use, the project was designed to serve two purposes. The solar panels produce electricity above ground, while sheep continue to graze on the grass beneath the supporting structures. Keating said the idea began nearly a decade ago as part of a long-term plan to protect his family's farm from changing economic conditions. "This project started back in 2017 with a simple vision to diversify our farm's income and build a sustainable, long-term legacy for my family and to also do our bit for the environment," Keating said at an open day held at the farm to mark the start of operations. "Bringing it to life required significant work across planning, the ESB grid connection and financing. Support from the Government's SRESS scheme, along with Flogas coming on board with a 15-year Power Purchase Agreement, was key to making the project bankable." Keating added: "I would also like to extend my sincere thanks to our project partners Bank of Ireland, the Strategic Banking Corporation of Ireland and PV Generation Ltd. It was the support of both, and in particular that of PV Generation Ltd, that was critical in making this milestone possible."Long-term contract provides commercial certaintyTo secure funding and ensure there would be a buyer for the electricity, Keating signed a 15-year Power Purchase Agreement with energy supplier Flogas, a subsidiary of DCC Energy plc. Under the agreement, Flogas will buy the renewable electricity produced by the farm and supply it to the national grid. Ken O'Byrne, managing director of Flogas Energy, said long-term commercial agreements can help small renewable energy projects move from the planning stage to full operation. "What makes Meadhill Solar Farm significant is that it shows how a long-term PPA can help a farmer-led renewable project move from an idea on paper to a fully operational asset," O'Byrne said. "Our role is to provide the commercial certainty that gives projects like this a route to market and helps unlock the investment needed to bring them forward." O'Byrne said Flogas believes the same business model could work for other farmers, small businesses, and independent energy developers in rural communities across Ireland.Government ministers highlight small-scale renewablesThe government's Small-Scale Renewable Energy Support Scheme supports clean energy projects that produce between 50 kW and 6 MW of electricity. It offers guaranteed payment rates to help community projects, small businesses, and farmers take part directly in the move towards renewable energy. Government ministers described the Cork farm as a practical example of how environmental goals can support rural businesses. "The Small-Scale Renewable Electricity Support Scheme is an important part of our strategy to increase renewable electricity generation across Ireland and to enable farmers, rural communities and smaller developers to participate in the energy transition," said Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment Darragh O'Brien in statements released about the project's launch. "Meadhill Solar Farm shows how the right policy framework can help turn locally developed ideas into operational renewable energy projects." Minister of State at the Department of Agriculture, Food and the Marine Niall Collins attended the open day in County Cork. He highlighted the financial benefits that diversification can bring to family farms. "For farming families, diversification is increasingly important in building sustainable businesses for the future," Collins said. "Meadhill Solar Farm is a practical example of how renewable energy can become part of that story, with Sean Keating continuing to farm the land while creating a new source of income for his family."You use AI every day. articles.summary: The chilling text for which a United Airlines flight bound for Newark, New Jersey, was forced to return to Las Vegas after the text was seen by a crew
articles.body: The chilling text for which a United Airlines flight bound for Newark, New Jersey, was forced to return to Las Vegas after the text was seen by a crew member has now been revealed. 25-year-old Dante Milne, a passenger, allegedly wrote that he was “gonna hijack this” plane, using an expletive, and would “crash ur row only,” according to a copy of the criminal complaint. The document does not specify how the messages were sent or who received them.The incident took place on Saturday night, October 24, aboard United Airlines Flight 1681, which had departed Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas for Newark Liberty International Airport. The flight was carrying 150 passengers.According to reports citing air traffic control audio, a flight attendant noticed the passenger texting about hijacking the aircraft and alerted the pilot. The crew then secured the cockpit and initiated a lockdown procedure.“The flight attendant saw him texting that he was going to hijack the aircraft. They called me. We went into lockdown, and we returned to Vegas,” the captain told air traffic controllers, according to an audio recording.When controllers asked whether the passenger was restrained or complying with instructions, the pilot said the man was unaware of what was happening and was cooperating.“The passenger does not know anything is going on,” the pilot said. “No restraint, passenger is compliant because he’s unaware.”The aircraft had taken off with enough fuel for its planned cross-country journey and could not immediately make a normal landing at its current weight. Reports said the plane flew in loops to burn off fuel before returning to Las Vegas.The aircraft landed safely at Harry Reid International Airport at around 11.05 pm local time. No injuries were reported.Passenger arrested over alleged threatsLas Vegas police detained the man following a report of “terroristic threats” aboard the flight. He was arrested on charges of making a threat or providing false information regarding an act of terrorism. Court records show he posted a $10,000 bond and was released pending a scheduled court appearance on Tuesday.The charge carries a possible prison sentence of one to 20 years.Flight delayed overnightUnited Airlines confirmed that the flight returned safely to Las Vegas to address a “potential security concern.”The diversion caused an overnight delay after the crew reached its permitted duty-time limit. The flight eventually departed for Newark on Sunday morning, October 25.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.body: Cheerios is giving its familiar cereal box an upgrade that could put an end to rolled-up bags, cereal clips and stale O's. The General Mills brand has teamed up with Ziploc to introduce Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal, a resealable bag inside a traditional cereal box. The company said Cheerios and Ziploc receive hundreds of thousands of requests, comments and reactions annually about cereal packaging. A December 2025 survey conducted by consumer insights platform Suzy revealed that 90% of cereal eaters take additional steps to preserve freshness after opening a box, including using clips, clothespins and cereal containers. "Cheerios with Ziploc PantrySeal takes a small, everyday cereal frustration and finally gives consumers the simple solution they've been asking for," Emilie Knox, vice president and business unit director for Cheerios at General Mills, said in a statement. People have been asking for ages," one Reddit user wrote earlier this year. articles.summary: The Texas midterm took an interesting turn after 21-year-old Vasant Bhatt, a student at the University of Houston, urged the Indian-American community to
articles.body: The Texas midterm took an interesting turn after 21-year-old Vasant Bhatt, a student at the University of Houston, urged the Indian-American community to reject the hatred against India and Hinduism and vote for Democrat James Talarico against Ken Paxton. Bhatt, who identified with conservative politics so far, was mocked online and asked to go back to India. MAGA activists defended their India-hatred, making Bhatt an example of how Indian-origin people who are US citizens by birth take the side of Indian-Americans and consider themselves Indian despite being born in the US. Bhatt was dropped from a conservative news website, Campus Reform, after his viral social media post.Speaking to TOI.com, Bhatt said his parents grew concerned about the amount of public attention his social media post got and the hostility he received thereafter. "Their primary concern has been my safety and well-being," the second-generation Indian-American said.Having interned with Ted Cruz's team earlier, Bhatt developed his alignment with conservative politics, but the India-hatred in Texas by MAGA drove him away. He is now politically homeless, though he said several Democratic political strategists reached out to him in the aftermath of the controversy. "I remain politically independent and my decision to speak out was entirely my own," Bhatt said.Can't be a perpetual foreigner at homeOn October 19, Bhatt announced that he cast his ballot for James Talarico. "As a second-generation Indian American, I am thoroughly disgusted by the xenophobia, racial resentment, and increasingly brazen attacks on my identity. My family has contributed to the American story through hard work, sacrifice, and an unwavering belief in the opportunities this nation promises. I am every bit as American as anyone else, and I will not tolerate being treated as a perpetual foreigner in the country I call home," he explained the reason and then urged every eligible Texan to go out and vote."This election is about the kind of state and country we are prepared to defend—and the principles we refuse to surrender," he added. He tagged Talarico's team and Texas Democrats in his post.Ken Paxton vs James TalaricoTexas saw historic turnout in the early voting, with more than 4.5 million voters already having cast their ballots. In five of six public polls released over the past week, Talarico leads Paxton. The sixth poll, from Fox News, puts both candidates at 49 percent. Kalshi traders gave Talarico a 65 percent chance of winning on Monday, and the site's margin market points to a win of about 2.2 points. articles.title: Museums hide mummies from public view due to lack of 'consent' from ancient Egyptians or their descendants
articles.summary: Glasgow museums removed ancient Egyptian mummies from display over consent concerns, citing a revised code of ethics on human remains dignity.
articles.body: Two museums in Scotland have reportedly removed ancient Egyptian mummies from public view out of concern that they were displayed without the consent of the deceased. Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum is one of several museums in Glasgow, Scotland, that have changed their policies on displaying human remains. The BBC reported that Glasgow Life, which manages Kelvingrove, removed the mummified remains of the Egyptian priest Nekht, who lived more than 3,500 years ago, along with his painted coffin, in the "absence of consent from the deceased individual or their descendants." A spokesperson for Glasgow Life told Fox News Digital, "The removal of human remains from display at Glasgow Life museums reflects contemporary museum practice." "The International Council of Museums’ revised Code of Ethics, published in June 2026, states that ‘Museums should uphold the inherent dignity of human remains and promote respect for their significance,’" the spokesperson continued. "The All-Party Parliamentary Group on Afrikan Reparations 2025 report, ‘Laying Ancestors to Rest,’ also raises ethical concerns about the display of ancient Egyptian human remains due to the consistent disregard of the potential wishes of the ancestors and the intention of the communities that originally laid them to rest." LIBERAL ARTS COLLEGE DROPS PROF’S NAME FROM CAMPUS HALL AFTER GRAVE DIG CONTROVERSY "Glasgow Life Museums’ draft Human Remains Policy proposes that human remains should only be displayed where there is documented and informed consent from the deceased individual or, in appropriate circumstances, their descendants," the spokesperson concluded. "In the absence of such consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals." The Hunterian, another museum in Glasgow, said the elaborate sarcophagus, or decorated coffin, of Lady Shep-En-Hor will remain on display, but her mummified remains will be covered going forward. When contacted by Fox News Digital, the Hunterian provided a press release which said, "As part of its commitment to becoming a more ethical institution, The Hunterian at the University of Glasgow is considering its holdings of archaeological and anatomical human remains across all sections of its collections." Museums have faced growing questions about the ownership and display of artifacts acquired from other countries, particularly during periods of Western colonial rule. The Hunterian's decision also raises questions about whether museums should treat human remains from the United Kingdom differently from those originating abroad. LOUVRE TURNS AWAY TOURISTS AS PARIS BRACES FOR RENEWED VIOLENCE FOLLOWING DESTRUCTIVE RIOTS "Human remains are among those items which The Hunterian seeks most keenly to return to their communities and nations of origin," the statement continued. "The Hunterian is also re-assessing what will be on display to the general public and, as part of its duty for the respectful care of these collections, it has decided to no longer put human remains from outside the UK on open display." "After in-depth consideration and consultation with experts, including Egyptologists, The Hunterian has decided to continue to display Lady Shep-En-Hor’s sarcophagus as a fine work of Late Period Ancient Egyptian funerary art, but to cover the mummified person, so she can no longer be viewed," the statement added, specifying that "The Hunterian takes the view that the Lady Shep-En-Hor deserves privacy in death." The decisions follow a revision to the International Council of Museums' (ICOM) Code of Ethics, which calls on museums to "uphold the inherent dignity of human remains and promote respect for their significance," according to the BBC report. "Decisions about these items and collections should be made in collaboration with descendants or communities from which they originate, if known," the ICOM guidance added. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Steph Scholten, a professor who serves on ICOM's ethics committee, told the BBC that the guidelines can be interpreted differently by institutions. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP "What the code of ethics puts forward is that these topics need careful consideration and decision making, they do not suggest one fixed outcome. Kelvingrove and The Hunterian have come to slightly different outcomes about our displays," he said. "The code of ethics does not prescribe that all human remains should be taken of display."

articles.title: In 2020, Taal’s eruption buried a Batangas home in ash; 15 days later, an eight-year-old dog named Idol was found alive beneath a wooden bed
articles.summary: In a miraculous rescue, Idol, an eight-year-old dog, was found alive 15 days after the Taal Volcano erupted, buried beneath volcanic ash in Batangas. The heartwarming story highlights the resilience of pets during natural disasters. Read more about Idol's survival and the impact of the Taal eruption.
articles.body: An eight-year-old dog was found alive beneath a wooden bed covered in volcanic ash 15 days after the Taal Volcano erupted in the Philippines. According to GMA News Online, the owners, Jay-R Balba and his brother Germie, discovered him at their home in San Nicolas, Batangas, after local officials permitted them to return. The rescue reunited Idol with his owners after more than two weeks in the damaged home, and the family took him and the other pets to Germie’s house, where they planned to stay.A search beneath the bed led to Idol’s rescueThe dog, named Idol, was barely able to move when the brothers rescued him and reportedly had been without food and water and appeared almost skin and bones. After he was freed, Idol drank several bowls of water and slowly regained his appetite, the same outlet reported. His survival came after the eruption forced the family to evacuate their home without taking their pets. Jay-R later recalled the wooden bed in his father’s room as Idol’s favourite resting place and decided to check the spot after local officials allowed residents to visit their homes.Other pets were also reunited with their owners after photos of them circulated on social media once some areas had been declared outside the danger zone. Animal welfare groups and pet rescue organisations were searching towns across Batangas for animals left behind as residents fled the eruption. Idol’s survival was remarkable given the circumstances in which animals were left without access to food, water, or care.Idol’s ordeal was part of a wider disaster Two studies published after the disaster, in IOP Conference Series and Scientific Reports, examined how Taal’s activity developed and how its effects spread across the surrounding environment. In a research study titled “Evolution, Causes and Influence Factors of Taal Volcanic Activities”, published in 2022, satellite imagery was used to compare conditions before and after the eruption. The findings provide context for the ash that covered homes and vegetation after the volcanic eruption.As per the 2022 study, the volcanic unrest was traced back to March 2019, when elevated seismic activity showed slight inflation and the amount of carbon dioxide flux increased. Seismic swarms happened in December, and a sequence of phreatic and phreatomagmatic activity was detected on the day of the eruption, followed by a rising alert level and evacuation measures. Taal was located near a convergent boundary between the Eurasian and Philippine Sea tectonic plates, where subduction contributed to volcanic activity.Based on the Sentinel-2 satellite images from before and after the eruption, the researchers were able to determine that the volcano island and nearby land had turned grey after the event, which indicated widespread volcanic deposits and a loss of visible plant cover. By April 2020, much of the vegetation outside the island had recovered, and in September, the island itself remained largely grey, with sparse vegetation.A second study, “Hazardous base surges of Taal’s 2020 eruption”, published in Scientific Reports in 2021, examined a more immediate physical danger. A. M. F. Lagmay and co-authors used field observations, satellite and drone imagery, LiDAR data and terrain models to analyse base surges. These were fast-moving, turbulent mixtures of hot gas and particles produced during explosive eruptions when magma interacted with water.The study found that the surges travelled at 50–60 metres per second near the crater rim, then slowed before reaching coastal communities. Researchers estimated that the deposits covered 6.2 square kilometres of Taal Volcano Island and had a total volume of about 19 million cubic metres. At the coast, deposits averaged 0.9 metres thick. The flows extended approximately 600 metres offshore near Calauit village. The research also documented severe losses among animals, with more than 1,000 livestock killed in the south-eastern part of the island. In Calauit, on the island, 480 families evacuated hours before it was overwhelmed, but there was insufficient time to move hundreds of cattle, horses, carabaos and goats, along with more than 1,000 pigs and poultry.You use AI every day. articles.title: AAP sarpanch’s son shot dead outside gurdwara near Amritsar
articles.summary: AAP sarpanch’s son Teerath Singh shot dead outside gurdwara near Amritsar; friend injured. Police cite land dispute; FIR names four suspects, no arrests yet.
articles.body: Amritsar: In the second public murder in Punjab in 24 hours, the son of an Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) sarpanch was shot dead and his friend injured outside a gurdwara near Amritsar on Monday evening.The shooting took place in Cheete Kalan village in Chatiwind on the outskirts of Amritsar. The deceased, Teerath Singh, was returning after paying obeisance at the gurdwara along with his friend Ranjit Singh when the gunmen opened fire, sparking panic in the area.The attackers fled as both friends collapsed on the roadside. Passersby took them to hospital where Teerath was declared dead. Ranjit is being treated for a bullet injury, and is out of danger, said Attari DSP Yadwinder Singh on Tuesday.Police sources said Teerath’s family suspects the involvement of a rival group from the village. Teerath’s brother Karaj Singh had also won the sarpanch election on an AAP ticket while their mother is the sarpanch.The DSP ruled out any political rivalry and said preliminary investigations suggest that the murder was triggered by an old animosity over a land dispute. Police have registered an FIR naming four suspects — Gurditt Singh, Gurjant Singh, Harkirat Singh alias Hockey, and Gora. No one had been arrested till Tuesday evening. Yadwinder said multiple teams are working on the case.The Cheete Kalan murder stunned the state as it was grappling with a double murder in Moga on Sunday evening.The latest killing triggered another round of political attacks on AAP govt, with former Union minister Ravneet Singh Bittu questioning its ability to maintain law and order in Punjab. In an X post he said, “The murder of Teerath Singh, brother of an incumbent AAP sarpanch, outside a gurdwara in Amritsar is a stark indictment of Punjab’s collapsed law and order. Not a single day passes without the state being shaken by gunfire. When even the ruling party’s own representatives and their families are not safe, the security of ordinary citizens is left in God’s hands. articles.title: Chicago cardinal sparks controversy by honoring abortion-access donor at gala for future priests
articles.summary: Chicago Cardinal Blase Cupich faces growing backlash for plans to honor Michael Sacks, whose family foundation gave $500,000 to Planned Parenthood.
articles.body: A prominent Catholic cardinal is facing backlash over plans to honor a wealthy Democratic donor who gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to organizations supporting abortion access at a fundraising gala benefiting the education of future priests. Chicago Cardinal Blase Cupich is scheduled to recognize billionaire Michael Sacks at the Oct. 29 Rerum Novarum Awards Dinner benefiting Mundelein Seminary, according to the event's announcement. Between 2020 and 2022, the Sacks Family Foundation, of which Sacks is president and treasurer, reportedly contributed grants totaling $500,000 to Planned Parenthood of Illinois, raising questions about the recognition in light of the Catholic Church's longstanding opposition to abortion. According to a report from Crain’s Chicago Business on Sept. 29, Sacks and his wife, Cari, gave $600,000 to the Prairie State Access Fund, an initiative established in partnership with the administration of Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to support abortion access in the state. Sacks is a board member of the Obama Foundation. EXCLUSIVE: PLANNED PARENTHOOD SET FOR MASSIVE TAXPAYER WINDFALL IF SENATE FAILS TO ACT The planned honor comes roughly a year after Cupich faced criticism from fellow Catholic leaders over plans to recognize Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., whose support for abortion rights drew objections from bishops who argued that honoring him would conflict with Church teaching. Durbin declined to accept the lifetime achievement award following the backlash. In a Monday statement defending the recognition for Sacks, Cupich wrote in part, "This year, the Nostra Aetate Award will be added to the honoring ceremony. It is named for the Declaration on the Relation of the Church to Non-Christian Religions, issued by the Second Vatican Council, and is designed to affirm the value the Church places on interreligious relationships by honoring members of non-Christian communities for their leadership in their own and the wider community. This year’s recipient is Mr. Michael Sacks, a well-respected leader in Chicago and in the Jewish community." Cupich further defended the decision, arguing that the Catholic Church's Nostra Aetate declaration provides a framework for honoring and building relationships with individuals who do not share Catholic beliefs, including those who hold differing moral or political views. He maintained that recognizing someone for their leadership and service to the community does not constitute an endorsement of all their positions, but instead fosters mutual respect and creates opportunities for meaningful dialogue. ‘BARBARIC’ ABORTION PROVISION FUELS CHRISTIAN PUSH TO CRACK DOWN ON DEM GOVERNOR Carl E. Olson, editor of the Catholic World Report, called out Cupich on X Monday, writing, "A pro-abortion billionaire is being given a prominent award by the @archchicago because he's ‘well-respected’ in Chicago and the Jewish community. In defending the choice, @CardinalBCupich plays the antisemitic card, saying, ‘Refusing to honor or engage with Jews solely because they hold conflicting religious or political positions can risk mimicking historic patterns of antisemitism through exclusion and bigotry, which, frighteningly, is on the rise.’" POPE LEO PROMOTES ARCHBISHOP WHO BARRED PELOSI FROM COMMUNION TO ONE OF VATICAN'S HIGHEST COURTS Olson added, "Surely there are prominent pro-life Jewish leaders in the Chicago area? Also, what if, theoretically, it were discovered that Mr. Sacks had given money to a pro-MAGA group? Would the antisemitic card still be used?" Catholic investigative reporter Christine Niles also took to X to raise concerns, sharing a quote from the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops' statement "Catholics in Political Life," which reads, "The Catholic community and Catholic institutions should not honor those who act in defiance of our fundamental moral principles. They should not be given awards, honors or platforms which would suggest support for their actions." In a statement to Fox News Digital, Kelsey Reinhardt, president and CEO of CatholicVote, said, "The U.S. bishops have taught that Catholic institutions should not give ‘awards, honors or platforms’ to those who act in defiance of our fundamental moral principles. A little over a year ago, Catholics made clear their disappointment that the Archdiocese of Chicago attempted to honor a public supporter of abortion." Reinhardt added, "We urge Cardinal Cupich to reconsider this honor. The pre-born babies and the faithful who support them cry out once again." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The media relations department for Cupich told Fox News Digital that it has nothing to add to the statement on its website. In a statement to Fox News Digital, a spokesperson for Sacks said, "Mr. Sacks is honored to receive the award and believes the Cardinal's statement speaks for itself." Fox News Digital reached out to the USCCB for comment.

articles.title: Goals are flowing, but for Chiki, wins must follow
articles.summary: Panaji: Christian Borrego was a big hit when he walked into the FC Goa headquarters in Porvorim on Tuesday.
articles.body: Panaji: Christian Borrego was a big hit when he walked into the FC Goa headquarters in Porvorim on Tuesday. He was there for a pre-match media interaction, but his presence made heads turn.Staffers stopped whatever they were doing. At least one sought his jersey, “whenever possible,” and there was some work to do for the club’s social media pages.Of course, there was a customary appeal to the fans too.All this not surprising for a player who is now the biggest attraction at the club. Christian, or Chiki as he is known, has scored in four consecutive matches for Goa, both in the domestic Indian Super League (ISL) and AFC Challenge League. The only time he did not find the back of the net was in the AFC Champions League Two playoff against FK Arkadag. But expecting a player to fire a day after joining training is too much of an ask.“I am enjoying the start, but this is a long journey,” Chiki told TOI. “I am very excited at scoring these goals because it’s important for a striker. But I think the most important is the team and our ability to secure victories. We must get wins for the team.”It’s not lost on anyone that Goa have won only one of their five competitive games this season. And Chiki is keen to turn things around, starting with the clash against SC Delhi at the Nehru Stadium in Fatorda on Wednesday.“In football, team is the most important part. I enjoy the thrill of scoring goals, but nothing matches the thrill of securing a win.
